analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited, undisclosed "soft money" contributions to political parties in federal elections.
analysis.headline: The soft money ban drew zero cosponsors, sat in committee with no hearing, and died at the end of the 103rd Congress without ever reaching the House floor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Federal Election Campaign Act so that "soft money" — the unlimited money that corporations, labor unions, and wealthy donors gave to political parties outside normal contribution limits and disclosure rules — counted as a regulated, publicly reported contribution. It also stripped out the provision that let unions and corporations spend on campaign communications beyond the federal limits. The bill was referred to the House Administration Committee in August 1993, never got a hearing or a cosponsor, and died when the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and small-dollar donors. The bill's own findings say banning soft money would make individual contributions from small donors the key to winning a federal campaign, and would put every federal election contribution under public disclosure rules instead of leaving over $750 million in 1992-cycle money unreported. Candidates who lacked access to corporate treasuries or union war chests would compete on a more even field.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the definitions of 'contribution' and 'expenditure' in the 1971 campaign finance law so that unlimited soft money given to political parties becomes a regulated contribution subject to the existing limits, closing the loophole parties used to raise and spend money beyond them.

Strikes the provision that let labor unions and corporations spend on campaign communications outside the federal ban, effectively eliminating corporate and union soft money as well as party soft money.

Per the bill's findings, eliminating soft money means every contribution to a federal election would be subject to federal disclosure requirements, so voters could see who is actually paying for campaigns.

The bill's findings state that soft money in the 1992 election cycle exceeded $750 million, with labor unions alone spending more than $400 million, and that this money carried no public reporting — money the ban would have brought into the open or off the table.

analysis.who_pays: Political parties lose their unregulated fundraising channel; labor unions and corporations lose their exemption from the ban on federal election spending, ending a combined flow the bill's findings put above $750 million in a single cycle. Wealthy donors and big institutional givers lose the ability to exceed contribution limits through party committees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Parties, labor unions, corporations, big donors

drawbacks.text: The ban would take away labor unions' main legal channel for federal political spending — the bill's own findings single out the more than $400 million unions spent in 1992 — so unions and their allies would lose money used to support candidates and mobilize voters, even if corporate money found other routes.

Because the ban works entirely by redrawing the statutory definitions of 'contribution' and 'expenditure' in the 1971 act, it does not cap total campaign spending; money that left the parties could shift to independent spending by outside groups, which the bill leaves largely untouched, weakening how much real change it delivers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have shut an unlimited, unreported money channel used by parties, unions, and corporations alike, and shifted influence toward small donors — a clear gain for transparency and ordinary voters. The real costs fall on unions and parties, which would lose funds for political activity, and the design has a gap: it redefines contribution and expenditure rules without touching independent spending, so determined money could move around it. Those are real but modest costs against a substantial gain in disclosure and contribution limits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Administration Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, and the committee never gave it a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Representative Christopher Cox, a California Republican, introduced the bill on August 6, 1993, framing soft money as special-interest money that was 'subverting the democratic principles' of the electoral process.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration — the standard first step that gave the committee control over whether it would move.
Not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor in the year and a half that followed.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind; the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The political parties and their biggest institutional funders — labor unions, corporations, and wealthy donors — kept an unlimited, unreported money channel open through the 1990s, and incumbents kept the incumbent-friendly system the bill's findings described.

for.name: Christopher Cox
for.what_they_did: Introduced the soft money ban and authored its findings, but attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Charlie Rose
against.role: Chair, House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: The bill sat in his committee for the rest of the Congress with no hearing, markup, or vote, so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: Members of the House, both parties
against.what_they_did: Not one member cosponsored the bill, from either party, over its 17-month life.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the lone sponsor was a Republican with zero cosponsors from either party, so the bill never drew enough support to reveal a partisan split.

industries.note: Soft money was the parties' unregulated funding channel — unlimited donations beyond the normal limits with no public reporting. The bill closes that channel, so the parties' financial interest lay in keeping it open, which put them against the disclosure and limits voters would have gained.

Section 3 strips the exemption that let unions fund campaign communications outside the federal ban, and the bill's findings single out the more than $400 million unions spent in the 1992 cycle. Unions had a direct financial stake in keeping that spending channel alive.

The same provision ends the corporate exemption for campaign communications spending, cutting off corporate soft money along with union soft money. Corporate givers' interest in unlimited undisclosed donations ran against the transparency the bill offered voters.
